clue.text: French memoirist in country residence of Nobel prizewinner

parts.note: a French country house or castle is a chateau
Aristide Briand, French statesman, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1926

explanation.surface: A French writer of memoirs is found living in the country house of a Nobel laureate.
explanation.walkthrough: François-René de Chateaubriand wrote the Mémoires d'outre-tombe; Briand shared the 1926 Peace Prize for the Locarno treaties.
explanation.definitionFit: The vicomte wrote the celebrated autobiography Memoirs from Beyond the Grave, so he is the French memoirist.

clue.text: Eunice had memo I revised, revealing Balzac oeuvre

indicators.note: something revised has been reworked, so these letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman named Eunice, having revised her memo, discloses a novel cycle by Balzac.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revised' rearranges the fourteen letters of EUNICE HAD MEMO I.
explanation.definitionFit: Balzac grouped his many novels and stories under the collective title of The Human Comedy, his life's work.

clue.text: What all colours will do in the dark, said Bacon

definitions.text: What all colours will do in the dark, said Bacon

parts.words: What all colours will do in the dark, said Bacon
parts.note: Francis Bacon's essay Of Unity in Religion says that in the dark all colours become indistinguishable, the verb being the missing word

explanation.walkthrough: Bacon's line runs 'All colours will agree in the dark'; the clue asks what the colours do.
explanation.definitionFit: In darkness colours look alike, so they concur or match, which is Bacon's verb for it.

clue.text: Is his work not expected to endure?

definitions.text: Is his work not expected to endure?

parts.words: Is his work not expected to endure?
parts.note: describes someone whose writings or studies concern short-lived things, made to last a day

explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from Greek for 'lasting a day'; it names a writer of short-lived pieces or a student of ephemera.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a person produces or studies transient things, so nobody expects the work to last.

clue.text: His work was missed, it's said

definitions.text: His work was missed, it's said

parts.words: His work was missed, it's said
parts.note: a Spanish author whose novel Niebla translates as Mist, which sounds like the word missed

explanation.walkthrough: Miguel de Unamuno's novel Niebla (1914) is known in English as Mist; 'it's said' marks the sound of 'missed'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Basque writer's best-known novel is Niebla, whose English title sounds just like the clue's word missed.

clue.text: Rogers's men, who failed to find the way to Japan

definitions.text: Rogers's men, who failed to find the way to Japan

parts.words: Rogers's men, who failed to find the way to Japan
parts.note: Major Robert Rogers's colonial irregulars, whose leader in Kenneth Roberts's novel Northwest Passage dreams of a route to the Orient

explanation.walkthrough: In Northwest Passage, Rogers longs to find the sea route through America to the East, and never does.
explanation.definitionFit: Rogers commanded a famous company of colonial scouts in the French and Indian War, known by his name.

clue.text: Prevost, for example, concealed in drab bedcovers

explanation.surface: A French cleric is found hiding in some dull bedclothes.
explanation.walkthrough: Antoine François Prévost, author of Manon Lescaut, was known by his clerical title, so he exemplifies the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A French abbot or cleric took this title, and the novelist Prévost was always styled with it.

clue.text: Silas dims badly in sacking

indicators.note: something done badly is botched, so the letters of the two words are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A man called Silas turns down the lights poorly while being fired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges the nine letters of SILAS DIMS.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sacked is being fired from a job, which is a discharge from employment.

clue.text: Old Nabokovian sinner offers flower to model, twice

explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' is the crossword's river; the narrator of Lolita has a doubled name.
explanation.definitionFit: Lolita's middle-aged narrator is a notorious predator, the great sinner of Nabokov's fiction.

clue.text: Military manoeuvre at sea from Waugh's Marquis

the main is a poetic word for the open sea

explanation.surface: A naval exercise at sea comes from an aristocrat in an Evelyn Waugh novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Marchmain is the Marquis of Brideshead Revisited.
explanation.definitionFit: In Brideshead Revisited the head of the Flyte family holds that marquisate.

clue.text: Head at University (Notre-Dame, presumably?)

explanation.surface: A head of a university department is perhaps a cathedral in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: Hugo's hunchback of Notre-Dame is in French 'le bossu', the hunchback, so the bracket hints at him.
explanation.definitionFit: In French the word means a hunchback, the most famous of whom lived in the Paris cathedral of Notre-Dame.

clue.text: Henry de Montherlant's fantasy ()

parts.note: Montherlant's first novel, Le Songe (1922), translates into English as this word for a vision in sleep

explanation.walkthrough: Le Songe was Montherlant's war novel; its title in English is also a word for fantasy.
explanation.definitionFit: A fantasy is a reverie or vision, and that English word translates the title of Montherlant's Le Songe.

clue.text: "Look in my face. My name is -to-was" (Henry Duff Traill)

explanation.definitionFit: The blank completes the parody's comic name, made from a past habit verb, in the line Traill wrote.

clue.text: The bailiff's daughter of Islington had a weary one in the ballad

explanation.walkthrough: The traditional ballad of the bailiff's daughter uses the phrase 'weary limb' for the walking girl.
explanation.definitionFit: A weary arm or leg is what a tired traveller wants to rest, the phrase used in the ballad.

explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' rearranges BERG and MAO together.
explanation.definitionFit: An official ban on trade with a country is the standard kind of prohibition this word names.

clue.text: The famous letter descended like a —— in the midst of the decorous council-chamber (Motley)

parts.note: a line from John Lothrop Motley's history of the Dutch Republic, where a letter lands with shattering surprise

explanation.walkthrough: The blank is a word for a shocking surprise, literally an explosive shell.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden shattering piece of news is likened to an exploding shell, hence the word in Motley's simile.

clue.text: He dispenses patronage in the modern world

definitions.text: He dispenses patronage in the modern world

parts.words: He dispenses patronage in the modern world

clue.text: Correct place of retirement in formal attire

explanation.surface: A retirement home is described as correct, in formal dress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'place of retirement' suggests a pensioner's home but means bed, where one retires for the night.
explanation.definitionFit: To edit copy as a newspaper's subeditor does is to correct it for publication.

clue.text: Valentino, king of Ruritania, we hear

clue.text: Fit, say, to be a murder victim

clue.text: Summer illumination from Faulkner
